messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Robert, a 57-year-old single man, presented for therapy with a quiet demeanor, the weight of years of silent struggle evident in his guarded posture. He spoke of an event that had fundamentally reshaped his life, an evening nearly a decade ago when he was sexually assaulted while walking home. He recalled the shocking jolt of being grabbed from behind, the suffocating pressure of a hand over his mouth, and the visceral terror of complete physical subjugation. The memory of the attacker’s breath on his neck, the rough texture of the fabric against his skin, and the overwhelming sensation of being utterly helpless, forced into compliance, remained chillingly vivid. Yet, other parts of the experience felt strangely fragmented; he knew what had happened, felt the truth of it deep in his bones, but found himself unable to string together a coherent narrative, grasping for words that simply wouldn't come to describe the full horror. It was as if he held a handful of intensely clear snapshots, but the story connecting them remained stubbornly out of reach.

In the years that followed, Robert’s world began to shrink. The assault had shattered his sense of safety, leaving him with a pervasive feeling that he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. He had come to believe that his own body could no longer be trusted, that it had somehow betrayed him by being vulnerable, and this feeling of unreliability extended to the world around him. He felt increasingly isolated, set apart from others by an experience he couldn't articulate, a burden he carried alone.

His occupation as a tutor, once a source of quiet satisfaction, became a minefield of potential triggers. He found himself constantly watching others, subtly scanning faces and body language for any hint of threat, particularly when alone with male students or parents. He instinctively sought out safe seats in any room, preferring a chair with his back to a wall, facing the door, allowing him to monitor all entrances and exits. The mere prospect of physical touch, even an innocent brush of hands while demonstrating a problem, would send a jolt of anxiety through him. He began to avoid in-person sessions whenever possible, increasingly opting for online tutoring, where he could control the distance and minimize the risk of any unwanted contact. When in-person meetings were unavoidable, he would meticulously arrange the space, ensuring a table always separated him from his student, maintaining a rigid personal boundary.

This hypervigilance and avoidance extended far beyond his work. He actively avoided unfamiliar places, explaining that he couldn't assess the danger effectively in new environments. His social life withered as he systematically dodged situations that made him feel strong emotions, preferring the predictable solitude of his apartment to the unpredictable interactions of social gatherings. If a conversation veered into emotionally charged territory, he would subtly change the subject or withdraw. His smoking habit, once occasional, had become a constant, a reliable ritual to dull the edge of his persistent anxiety and the crushing weight of his isolation. He recognized that he was increasingly alone, but the thought of letting anyone get close, of being touched or vulnerable again, was terrifying.

Recently, a male student, frustrated with a difficult concept, had inadvertently reached out to tap Robert's arm for emphasis. The sudden, unexpected physical contact, combined with the student’s raised voice, had sent Robert into a panic, forcing him to abruptly end the session. The incident had left him shaken for days, reinforcing his belief that he simply couldn't trust situations or people. It was this cumulative burden, the exhaustion of constant vigilance, the gnawing loneliness, and the realization that his carefully constructed world was still so fragile, that finally prompted Robert to seek help. He arrived at therapy not knowing if he could ever truly feel safe again, but with a desperate, quiet hope that perhaps, some of the fear could finally recede.
